Couples

Can passion last in a long relationship?

Intense infatuation tends to calm down, but some couples keep romantic love alive for decades.

At the start of a relationship everything is intense: we think about the other person all the time, we desire them and anything done together seems exciting. Over the years, that intensity usually fades. Is it inevitable that love turns into mere affection and habit?

What research says

Psychology distinguishes between passionate love, with intense desire and some obsession, and companionate love, based on intimacy and commitment. The first usually declines over time. But Bianca Acevedo and Arthur Aron reviewed many studies in 2009 and found that some long-term couples maintain intense romantic love, with interest and desire, though without the obsession of the early months. That kind of love was associated with greater satisfaction.

What helps? One of the most replicated findings is shared novelty. In a 2000 experiment, Aron and colleagues asked couples to do a new, somewhat exciting activity together; afterwards they were more satisfied with their relationship than couples who did something pleasant but routine.

From passionate love to companionate love

Elaine Hatfield distinguished between passionate love, intense and full of desire and thoughts about the other person, and companionate love, made of affection, trust and intimacy. The first usually declines in the early years of living together; the second can grow over time. This is not failure: it is the usual course. Even so, a study by Bianca Acevedo found that around one in ten long-term couples still showed intense love, without the obsession of the early days.

Celebrating your partner's good news

Shelly Gable studied how partners respond when one shares good news. The response that most strengthens the relationship is active and constructive: showing interest, asking questions, being genuinely glad ("that's great! how did they tell you?"). Responding with indifference or pointing out the downsides cools the relationship more than it seems. How you react to the good matters as much as how you support in the bad.

What usually helps

  • Do new things together: a trip, a class, a different plan.
  • Show genuine interest in what the other person tells you, including the small things.
  • Look after physical intimacy, without reducing it to sex.
  • Celebrate your partner's good news: responding enthusiastically to their achievements strengthens the relationship.

References

  1. Acevedo, B. P. y Aron, A. (2009). Does a long-term relationship kill romantic love? Review of General Psychology, 13(1), 59–65.
  2. Aron, A. et al. (2000). Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273–284.
  3. Gable, S. L. et al. (2004). What do you do when things go right? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228–245.
  4. Hatfield, E. y Walster, G. W. (1978). A New Look at Love. Reading (MA): Addison-Wesley.
  5. Acevedo, B. P. y Aron, A. (2009). Does a long-term relationship kill romantic love? Review of General Psychology, 13(1), 59–65.
